claim: Cortical neurons integrate thousands of synaptic inputs in their dendrites in highly nonlinear ways.
source: Cortical neurons integrate thousands of synaptic inputs in their dendrites in highly nonlinear ways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about cortical neurons.

claim: Dendritic nonlinearities are critical for the efficient integration of synaptic inputs in circuits performing analog computations with spiking neurons.
source: Here, we show that dendritic nonlinearities are critical for the efficient integration of synaptic inputs in circuits performing analog computations with spiking neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: A neuron's optimal dendritic nonlinearity for integrating synaptic inputs depends on the statistics of its presynaptic activity patterns.
source: We developed a theory that formalizes how a neuron's dendritic nonlinearity that is optimal for integrating synaptic inputs depends on the statistics of its presynaptic activity patterns.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework developed by the authors as stated in the abstract.

claim: The theory accurately predicted the responses of two different types of cortical pyramidal cells to patterned stimulation by two-photon glutamate uncaging based on their in vivo presynaptic population statistics.
source: Based on their in vivo preynaptic population statistics (firing rates, membrane potential fluctuations, and correlations due to ensemble dynamics), our theory accurately predicted the responses of two different types of cortical pyramidal cells to patterned stimulation by two-photon glutamate uncaging.
evidence: This is an experimental validation of the theory stated in the abstract.

claim: Dendritic integration can result in markedly sublinear integration of synaptic inputs.
source: The dendritic tree of a cortical neuron performs a highly nonlinear transformation on the thousands of inputs it receives from other neurons, sometimes resulting in a markedly sublinear (Longordo et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dendritic integration can result in strongly superlinear integration of synaptic inputs.
source: and often in strongly superlinear integration of synaptic inputs (Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Nevian et al., 2007; Branco and Häusser, 2011; Makara and Magee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Dendrites of cortical neurons carry out a remarkable repertoire of arithmetic operations including additive, multiplicative and divisive ways of combining individual synaptic inputs.
source: These nonlinearities have been traditionally studied from the perspective of single-neuron computations, using a few well-controlled synaptic stimuli, revealing a remarkable repertoire of arithmetic operations that the dendrites of cortical neurons carry out (Poirazi and Mel, 2001; London and Häusser, 2005; Branco et al., 2010) including additive, multiplicative and divisive ways of combining individual synaptic inputs in the cell's response (Silver, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Nonlinear dendritic integration actively shapes responses of single neurons under in vivo conditions in the hippocampus.
source: More recently, the role of nonlinear dendritic integration in actively shaping responses of single neurons under in vivo conditions has been demonstrated in several cortical areas including the hippocampus (Grienberger et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nonlinear dendritic integration actively shapes responses of single neurons under in vivo conditions in visual cortices.
source: as well as visual (Smith et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nonlinear dendritic integration actively shapes responses of single neurons under in vivo conditions in somatosensory cortices.
source: and somatosensory cortices (Xu et al., 2012; Lavzin et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Many of the basic biophysical mechanisms underlying dendritic nonlinearities are well understood.
source: However, while many of the basic biophysical mechanisms underlying these nonlinearities are well understood (Stuart et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It has proven a daunting task to include all biophysical mechanisms of dendritic nonlinearities in larger scale network models to understand their interplay at the level of the circuit.
source: it has proven a daunting task to include all these mechanisms in larger scale network models to understand their interplay at the level of the circuit (Herz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Studies of cortical computation and dynamics have largely ignored the complex and highly nonlinear information processing capabilities of the dendritic tree.
source: Conversely, studies of cortical computation and dynamics have largely ignored the complex and highly nonlinear information processing capabilities of the dendritic tree and concentrated on circuit-level computations emerging from interactions between point-like neurons with single, somatic nonlinearities (Hopfield, 1984; Seung and Sompolinsky, 1993; Gerstner and Kistler, 2002; Vogels et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: It is unknown how dendritic nonlinearities in individual cells contribute to computations at the level of a neural circuit.
source: Therefore, it is unknown how dendritic nonlinearities in individual cells contribute to computations at the level of a neural circuit.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Most theories of nonlinear dendritic integration focus on highly simplified input regimes, essentially requiring both the inputs and the output of a cell to have stationary firing rates.
source: A limitation of most theories of nonlinear dendritic integration is that they focus on highly simplified input regimes (Mel et al., 1998; Poirazi et al., 2003; Archie and Mel, 2000; Poirazi and Mel, 2001; Ujfalussy et al., 2009), essentially requiring both the inputs and the output of a cell to have stationary firing rates.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Most theories of nonlinear dendritic integration ignore the effects and consequences of temporal variations in neural activities at the time scale of inter-spike intervals characteristic of in vivo states in cortical populations.
source: This approach thus ignores the effects and consequences of temporal variations in neural activities at the time scale of inter-spike intervals characteristic of in vivo states in cortical populations (Crochet et al., 2011; Haider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The principle of 'adaptation to natural input statistics' has been highly successful in accounting for the input-output relationships of cells in a number of sensory areas at the systems level.
source: In contrast, we propose an approach which is specifically centered on these naturally occurring statistical patterns – in analogy to the principle of 'adaptation to natural input statistics' which has been highly successful in accounting for the input-output relationships of cells in a number of sensory areas at the systems level (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cortical neurons mainly communicate by action potentials, which are temporally punctate all-or-none events.
source: Our theory is based on the observation that cortical neurons mainly communicate by action potentials, which are temporally punctate all-or-none events.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about cortical neurons.

claim: The computations cortical circuits perform are commonly assumed to involve the transformations of analog activities varying continuously in time, such as firing rates or membrane potentials.
source: In contrast, the computations cortical circuits perform are commonly assumed to involve the transformations of analog activities varying continuously in time, such as firing rates or membrane potentials (Rumelhart et al., 1986; Hopfield, 1984; Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Archie and Mel, 2000; London et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The discrete and stochastic firing of spikes by neurons conveys only a limited amount of information about their rapidly fluctuating activities.
source: This implies a fundamental bottleneck in cortical computations: the discrete and stochastic firing of spikes by neurons conveys only a limited amount of information about their rapidly fluctuating activities (Pfister et al., 2010; Sengupta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The robust operation of a circuit requires its neurons to integrate their inputs in highly nonlinear ways that specifically depend on the computation performed by the neuron and the long-term statistics of the inputs it receives from its presynaptic partners.
source: Formalising the implications of this bottleneck mathematically reveals that the robust operation of a circuit requires its neurons to integrate their inputs in highly nonlinear ways that specifically depend on two complementary factors: the computation performed by the neuron and the long-term statistics of the inputs it receives from its presynaptic partners.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the mathematical formalism.

claim: The form of optimal input integration for presynaptic correlations can be efficiently approximated by a canonical, biophysically-motivated model of dendritic integration.
source: Next, to provide biophysical insight, we demonstrate that the form of optimal input integration for these presynaptic correlations can be efficiently approximated by a canonical, biophysically-motivated model of dendritic integration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis.

claim: NMDA receptor activation is necessary for dendritic integration to approximate the optimal response.
source: We also show that NMDA receptor activation is necessary for dendritic integration to approximate the optimal response.
evidence: This is shown through experimental data.

claim: Linear integration is optimal when presynaptic neurons are statistically independent.
source: In the first case (Figure 1C), when the presynaptic neurons were independent, the best linear response was identical to the optimal response.
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When presynaptic neurons are correlated, the optimal response becomes nonlinear and the best linear response is unable to accurately follow the fluctuations in the input.
source: However, if presynaptic neurons became correlated, the optimal response became nonlinear and the best linear response was unable to accurately follow the fluctuations in the input (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sublinear integration is optimal when presynaptic activities exhibit Gaussian random walks and do not contain statistical dependencies beyond second order correlations.
source: In particular, sublinear integration was optimal when presynaptic activities exhibited Gaussian random walks and thus they did not contain statistical dependencies beyond second order correlations (Figure 2A-C), as seen in the retina and cortical cultures (Schneidman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 2A-C, with support from a citation.

claim: Supralinear integration is optimal when the presynaptic population exhibits coordinated switches between distinct states associated with large differences in the activity levels compared to activity-fluctuations within each state.
source: In contrast, supralinear integration was optimal when the presynaptic population exhibited coordinated switches between distinct states associated with large differences in the activity levels compared to activity-fluctuations within each state (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Coordinated switches in presynaptic populations lead to higher order statistical dependencies as seen in the cortex in vivo, either due to population-wide modulation by cortical state or due to stimulus-driven activation of particular cell ensembles.
source: These switches led to higher order statistical dependencies as seen in the cortex in vivo, either due to population-wide modulation by cortical state (Gentet et al., 2010; Crochet et al., 2011), or due to stimulus-driven activation of particular cell ensembles (Harris et al., 2003; Ohiorhenuan et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Optimal input integration remains nonlinear even if the postsynaptic neuron computes a function of the presynaptic firing rates which are linearly related to spikes.
source: Moreover, optimal input integration remained nonlinear even if the postsynaptic neuron computed a function of the presynaptic firing rates (rather than membrane potentials) which were linearly related to spikes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purely passive dendritic properties lead to sublinear integration.
source: Indeed, the basic biophysical mechanisms present in dendrites naturally yield nonlinearities that are qualitatively similar to those of the optimal response: purely passive properties lead to sublinear integration (Koch, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Locally generated dendritic spikes endow dendrites with strong supralinearities.
source: whereas locally generated dendritic spikes endow dendrites with strong supralinearities (Nevian et al., 2007; Branco and Häusser, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A simple, biophysically-motivated, canonical model of nonlinear dendritic integration is able to produce responses that are near-identical to the optimal response for any sequence of presynaptic spikes when the statistics of a large presynaptic population are strongly dominated by the simultaneous switching of presynaptic neurons between a quiescent and an active state.
source: In this limiting case we were able to show mathematically (see Materials and methods) that a simple, biophysically-motivated, canonical model of nonlinear dendritic integration (Poirazi and Mel, 2001) is able to produce responses that are near-identical to the optimal response for any sequence of presynaptic spikes (Figure 3A, see also Figures 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The optimal response for presynaptic populations fully characterized by second-order correlations can be well approximated by a sigmoidal nonlinearity parametrized to be dominantly saturating.
source: In this case, the same type of dendritic model, but with a sublinear input-output mapping, was able to approximate the optimal response very closely. Although a closed-form solution for the optimal nonlinear mapping could not be obtained in this case, it could be shown to be sublinear (Appendix), and was well approximated by a sigmoidal nonlinearity parametrized to be dominantly saturating (Figures 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and shown in Figures 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The same type of sigmoidal nonlinearity can implement supralinear and sublinear integration depending on the input regime.
source: We also noted that it was the same type of sigmoidal nonlinearity which could implement supralinear and sublinear integration depending on the input regime (low background, synchronous spikes: supralinear; high background, asynchronous spikes: sublinear integration, compare Figure 3A and B, inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Dendritic integration may adapt to systematic changes in presynaptic statistics without having to change the parameters of its nonlinearity.
source: This suggests that dendritic integration may adapt to systematic changes in presynaptic statistics, such as those brought about by transitioning between the desynchronized and synchronized states of the neocortex, or sharp waves and theta activity in the hippocampus, without having to change the parameters of its nonlinearity (Borst et al., 2005) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by a citation and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dendritic integration in hippocampal pyramidal cells is supralinear when inputs are highly synchronized and linear if the input is asynchronous.
source: Indeed, Gasparini and Magee (2006) demonstrated that dendritic integration in hippocampal pyramidal cells was supralinear when inputs were highly synchronized (as they are during sharp waves), while integration was linear if the input was asynchronous (such as during theta activity).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The model with nonlinear dendrites and clustered connectivity had near-optimal cross-validated performance.
source: The model with nonlinear dendrites and clustered connectivity had near-optimal cross-validated performance (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The clustering of correlated inputs together with nonlinearities akin to those found in dendrites is necessary to achieve optimal estimation performance in the face of presynaptic correlations.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the clustering of correlated inputs together with nonlinearities akin to those found in dendrites is necessary to achieve optimal estimation performance in the face of presynaptic correlations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: The precision of predictions of the optimal response tuned to correct presynaptic statistics was not statistically different from that expected from the inherent variability of responses in individual dendrites for neocortical neurons.
source: We quantified the quality of match between the predicted and experimentally recorded time course of responses across a population of n = 6 (neocortex) and n = 6 (hippocampus) dendrites under a range of conditions varying ISI or the number of stimuli, and found that the precision of our predictions was not statistically different from that expected from the inherent variability of responses in individual dendrites (Figure 5E,J; neocortex: t = 0.2, P = 0.85
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The precision of predictions of the optimal response tuned to correct presynaptic statistics was not statistically different from that expected from the inherent variability of responses in individual dendrites for hippocampal neurons.
source: hippocampus: t = 1.85, P = 0.12).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: When the optimal response was tuned to unrealistic presynaptic statistics characterized purely by second-order correlations, the quality of fits became significantly worse for neocortical neurons.
source: In contrast, when the optimal response was tuned to unrealistic presynaptic statistics characterized purely by second-order correlations (cor2), or by a lack of any correlations implying statistically independent presynaptic firing (ind), the quality of fits became significantly worse (Figure 5E,J; neocortex: t = −4.6, P = 0.006 for cor2
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: When the optimal response was tuned to unrealistic presynaptic statistics characterized by a lack of any correlations, the quality of fits became significantly worse for neocortical neurons.
source: and t = −4.9, P = 0.004 for ind
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: When the optimal response was tuned to unrealistic presynaptic statistics characterized purely by second-order correlations, the quality of fits became significantly worse for hippocampal neurons.
source: hippocampus: t = −4, P = 0.01 for cor2
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: When the optimal response was tuned to unrealistic presynaptic statistics characterized by a lack of any correlations, the quality of fits became significantly worse for hippocampal neurons.
source: and t = −4.9, P = 0.004 for ind).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Using realistic presynaptic statistics matching hippocampal rather than neocortical activities resulted in significantly worse fits for neocortical responses.
source: Moreover, using realistic presynaptic statistics, but matching hippocampal rather than neocortical activities, also resulted in significantly worse fits for neocortical responses (Figures 5E; t= −3.6, P = 0.02).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Using realistic presynaptic statistics matching neocortical rather than hippocampal activities did not result in significantly worse fits for hippocampal responses.
source: The converse was not observed in the case of hippocampal neurons (Figures 5J; t= 0.43, P = 0.68).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Dendritic nonlinearities in cortical pyramidal neurons are specifically tuned to the dynamics of their presynaptic cortical ensembles.
source: This suggests that dendritic nonlinearities in cortical pyramidal neurons are specifically tuned to the dynamics of their presynaptic cortical ensembles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The blockade of NMDA receptor activation by AP5 resulted in dendritic responses that afforded substantially poorer fits by the model, even after refitting the postsynaptic parameters.
source: Furthermore, the blockade of NMDA receptor activation by AP5 resulted in dendritic responses that afforded substantially poorer fits by the model, even after refitting the postsynaptic parameters (Figure 5E,J, AP5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data and shown in Figure 5E,J.

claim: The fine tuning of dendritic nonlinearities to input statistics relies on the action of NMDA receptors.
source: This indicated that the fine tuning of dendritic nonlinearities to input statistics relied on the action of NMDA receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Assuming simple second-order correlations made the optimal response a close match to dendritic responses in cerebellar stellate cells.
source: In this case, we fitted the statistics of individual presynaptic cells to those of cerebellar granule cells. The correlations between these cells are less known, but we found that assuming simple second-order correlations made the optimal response a close match to dendritic responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of experimental data.

claim: Hippocampal- or neocortical-like statistics resulted in a substantially poorer fit in cerebellar stellate cells compared to second-order correlations.
source: In contrast, the hippocampal- or neocortical-like statistics that were crucial for matching responses in cortical dendrites (Figure 5D,H) resulted in a substantially poorer fit in this cerebellar cell type.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 5D,H.

claim: It is unlikely that the optimal response is implemented by the postsynaptic neuron as such due to its computational complexity.
source: Thus, it is unlikely to be implemented by the postsynaptic neuron as such.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational complexity of the optimal response.

claim: Simple second order correlations between presynaptic neurons imply sublinear integration which can be implemented by the saturating nonlinearity characteristic of passive dendrites.
source: We found that simple second order correlations between presynaptic neurons imply sublinear integration which can be implemented by the saturating nonlinearity characteristic of passive dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The biophysical substrate for the type of supralinear integration that was optimal for state-switching dynamics likely involves NMDA receptors.
source: Conversely, the biophysical substrate for the type of supralinear integration that was optimal for state-switching dynamics likely involves NMDA receptors because the particular dendritic nonlinearites observed in the cortical cells in which we tested our theory are known to be mediated primarily through NMDA receptor activation (Branco et al., 2010; Makara and Magee, 2013; Major et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Local plateau potentials generated by NMDA currents have been shown to have graded response durations.
source: Moreover, the local plateau potentials generated by NMDA currents have been shown to have graded response durations (Major et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The resulting nonlinearities from NMDA currents could be continuously tuned between weaker and stronger forms (boosting and bistability).
source: and the resulting nonlinearities could be continuously tuned between weaker and stronger forms (boosting and bistability, Major et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NMDA receptor mediated dendritic nonlinearities are ideally suited for being matched to presynaptic statistics.
source: These properties make NMDA receptor mediated dendritic nonlinearities ideally suited for being matched to presynaptic statistics, as the optimal response involves sustained dendritic depolarisations of varying duration (Figure 4) that depend parametrically on those statistics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the properties of NMDA receptors and the optimal response shown in Figure 4.

claim: The theory predicts the existence of a tight relationship between the structure of correlations in the activity of presynaptic cells and the morphological clustering of their synapses on the postsynaptic dendrite.
source: A central prediction of our theory that awaits confirmation is the existence of a tight relationship between the structure of correlations in the activity of presynaptic cells and the morphological clustering of their synapses on the postsynaptic dendrite.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the theory.

claim: The theory requires nonlinear integration of inputs from neurons with statistically dependent activity, while spikes from independent neurons need to be integrated linearly.
source: This is because our theory requires nonlinear integration of inputs from neurons with statistically dependent activity, while spikes from independent neurons need to be integrated linearly.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement of the theory.

claim: When synchronous, nearby inputs on the same dendritic branch are summed nonlinearly, whereas widely separated inputs are combined linearly.
source: Biophysical considerations suggest (Koch, 1999) and experimental data supports (Polsky et al., 2004; Losonczy and Magee, 2006) that, when synchronous, nearby inputs on the same dendritic branch are summed nonlinearly, whereas widely separated inputs are combined linearly.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The theory predicts that the correlation structure of the inputs will be mapped to the dendritic tree in a way that presynaptic neurons with strongly correlated activities target nearby locations while independent neurons innervate distinct dendritic subunits.
source: Consequently, our theory predicts that the correlation structure of the inputs will be mapped to the dendritic tree in a way that presynaptic neurons with strongly correlated activities target nearby locations while independent neurons innervate distinct dendritic subunits.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the theory.

claim: The kind of correlation relevant for determining synaptic clustering is the 'marginal' correlations between the membrane potentials of presynaptic neurons.
source: According to our theory, the kind of correlation relevant for determining synaptic clustering is the 'marginal' correlations between the membrane potentials of presynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the theory.

claim: Marginal correlations include both signal and noise correlations.
source: Marginal correlations include both signal and noise correlations (Averbeck et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Marginal correlations can reach substantial magnitudes even when noise correlations alone are small, especially for neurons with overlapping receptive fields.
source: and thus can reach substantial magnitudes even when noise correlations alone are small, as e.g. during desynchronized cortical states (Renart et al., 2010), especially for neurons with overlapping receptive fields (Froudarakis et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Marginal correlations are larger when measured between the membrane potentials of neurons rather than their spike counts.
source: and when measured between the membrane potentials of neurons rather than their spike counts (Dorn and Ringach, 2003; de la Rocha et al., 2007; Poulet and Petersen, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The segregation of different input pathways along the dendritic tree of hippocampal neurons supports the prediction of synaptic clustering at the level of different dendritic regions.
source: At the level of different dendritic regions, the segregation of different input pathways along the dendritic tree of hippocampal neurons supports this prediction (Witter et al., 1989; Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High resolution imaging revealed subcellular topography of sensory inputs in the tadpole visual system.
source: High resolution imaging revealed subcellular topography of sensory inputs in the tadpole visual system (Bollmann and Engert, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: High resolution imaging revealed clustered patterns of axonal activity in the parallel fibres that provide input to cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: clustered patterns of axonal activity in the parallel fibres that provide input to cerebellar Purkinje cells (Wilms and Häusser, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Experience-driven synaptic clustering has been demonstrated in the barn owl auditory localization pathway.
source: and experience-driven synaptic clustering in the barn owl auditory localization pathway (McBride et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neighboring synapses are more likely to be coactive than synapses that are further away from each other in developing hippocampal pyramidal cells.
source: Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that neighboring synapses are more likely to be coactive than synapses that are further away from each other in developing hippocampal pyramidal cells (Kleindienst et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neighboring synapses are more likely to be coactive than synapses that are further away from each other in hippocampal cultures and in vivo in the barrel cortex during spontaneous activity.
source: as well as in hippocampal cultures and in vivo in the barrel cortex during spontaneous activity (Takahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An interspersion of differently tuned orientation-, frequency- or whisker-specific synaptic inputs on the same dendritic segments was found in the mouse visual, auditory or somatosensory cortex, respectively.
source: In contrast, an interspersion of differently tuned orientation-, frequency- or whisker-specific synaptic inputs on the same dendritic segments was found in the mouse visual, auditory or somatosensory cortex, respectively, thus challenging the prevalence of synaptic clustering (Jia et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011; Varga et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The theory predicts clustering based on the long-term statistical dependencies between the responses of the presynaptic neurons for naturalistic inputs, which can be quite poorly predicted from their tuning properties for single stimulus dimensions.
source: In particular, our theory predicts clustering based on the long-term statistical dependencies between the responses of the presynaptic neurons for naturalistic inputs, which can be quite poorly predicted from their tuning properties for single stimulus dimensions (Harris et al., 2003; Fiser et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a prediction of the theory supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The statistical dependencies relevant for the theory are well represented by those found during spontaneous activity.
source: In contrast, the statistical dependencies relevant for our theory are well represented by those found during spontaneous activity (Berkes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Studies finding evidence in favor of synaptic clustering analyzed the structure of synaptic input to dendritic branches during spontaneous network activity.
source: Indeed, studies finding evidence in favor of synaptic clustering analyzed the structure of synaptic input to dendritic branches during spontaneous network activity (McBride et al., 2008; Kleindienst et al., 2011; Makino and Malinow, 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The basal dendrites of neocortical layer 2/3 pyramidal cells are targeted by neighbouring pyramidal neurons as well as by neurons from layer 4.
source: The basal dendrites of neocortical layer 2/3 pyramidal cells are targeted by neighbouring pyramidal neurons as well as by neurons from layer 4 (Douglas and Martin, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the hippocampal experiments, synapses on the proximal dendrites of CA3 neurons targeted by recurrent collaterals of neighbouring pyramidal cells were stimulated.
source: In the hippocampal experiments we stimulated synapses on the proximal dendrites of CA3 neurons targeted by recurrent collaterals of neighbouring pyramidal cells (Andersen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The presynaptic statistics for hippocampal neurons were fitted to in vivo population activity patterns recorded from the hippocampus during quiet wakefulness, characterised by sharp wave (SPW) activity.
source: We fitted the presynaptic statistics to in vivo population activity patterns recorded from the hippocampus during quiet wakefulness, characterised by sharp wave (SPW) activity (Csicsvari et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The presynaptic statistics for hippocampal neurons were fitted to awake extracellular data from CA3 and intracellular data from CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: As intracellular recordings from CA3 pyramidal neurons during SPW activity in the awake animal are not available, we fitted the presynaptic statistics to awake extracellular data from CA3 (Csicsvari et al., 2000; Grosmark et al., 2012) and intracellular (Ylinen et al., 1995; English et al., 2014) data from CA1 pyramidal neurons (Tables 1 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
